---
title: "Following evolution with the canonical equation"
subtitle: "Leaf mass per area and height at maturation evolving together in FF16"
format: html
---



[Finding evolutionary attractors](solving_attractors.qmd) locates the trait
values where selection stops by solving for a zero selection gradient. That
says where evolution can end, but not how it gets there, or whether it gets
there at all from a given start. The **canonical equation** of adaptive
dynamics follows the path [@Dieckmann-1996]. Each resident's traits move up
their selection gradient at a speed set by the supply of mutations:

$$
\frac{dz}{dt} = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mu\,\tilde n\,V\,\nabla_z s(z),
$$

where $z$ are the traits on the scale the search uses (here the logarithm of
each trait), $\mu$ the mutation rate, $\tilde n$ the resident's equilibrium
density relative to where it started, $V$ the mutational covariance and
$\nabla_z s$ the selection gradient. Every evaluation of the right-hand side
re-solves the community to demographic equilibrium, so one evaluation costs
one `plant` equilibrium plus one selection gradient.

When the gradient vanishes, `regnans` checks whether the resident sits at a
fitness minimum. If it does, the lineage branches into two and the equation
carries on with both. If it does not, the end point is evolutionarily stable
and the run stops.

## Set up the community

Two traits evolve: leaf mass per area (`lma`) and height at maturation
(`hmat`). Patches last at most 30 years, which halves the run time against
the default 60 (the attractor depends on this choice).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(plant)
library(regnans)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

community0 <- community_start(
  bounds(lma = c(0.02, 0.6), hmat = c(2, 40)),
  model_support = list(
    p = plant_default_assembly_pars(max_patch_lifetime = 30),
    plant_control = plant_default_assembly_control()
  ),
  derivative_control = list(d_second = 1e-2, eps_second = 1e-2)
)
```
:::


The `derivative_control()` setting is about cost, not the answer. The stepper
below needs the Jacobian of the right-hand side, which `regnans` finds by
differencing selection gradients across equilibrium solves. Each of those
solves is converged to the cube of the relative step, so a step of `1e-2`
needs solves only to `1e-6`, against `1e-9` at the default `1e-3`. The run
reaches the same end point about a quarter faster.

## Integrate the canonical equation

Start from thin, cheap leaves on a short plant (`lma = 0.15`, `hmat = 6`):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce <- community_canonical_equation(
  community0,
  x0 = c(0.15, 6),
  control = canonical_control(list(stepper = "rodas"))
)

ce$outcome
#> [1] "stable"
ce$events
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>    time event  lineage
#>   <dbl> <chr>    <int>
#> 1 2823. polish      NA
#> 2 2823. stable      NA
```
:::


`stepper = "rodas"` is the default; it is written out here because it
matters. The two traits evolve on very different time scales: `lma` settles
within a few units of evolutionary time, while `hmat` takes thousands. A
system like this is **stiff**. An explicit stepper such as Cash–Karp
(`"rkck"`) is held to steps short enough for the fast `lma` direction long
after `lma` has stopped moving: on this problem it took 200 steps and eight
times the equilibrium solves without arriving. RODAS, a linearly implicit
stepper, takes steps as long as the slow `hmat` direction allows, and gets
there in 17.

As the gradients become small, the run finishes the approach by solving for
the stationary point directly (the `polish` event) rather than following an
ever-slower trajectory. The `stable` event means the branching test found no
fitness minimum there, so this pair of traits is evolutionarily stable.

The end point:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
final <- ce$trajectory[nrow(ce$trajectory), ]
final[, c("time", "lma", "hmat", "density", "gradient_lma", "gradient_hmat")]
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>    time    lma  hmat density gradient_lma gradient_hmat
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 2823. 0.0473  10.9    37.9 -0.000000691      -4.86e-9
```
:::


## The path

Over evolutionary time, `lma` falls quickly while `hmat` barely moves,
overshooting a little below where it ends. Then `hmat` rises slowly, and
`lma` creeps back up as taller plants favour slightly denser leaves:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ce$trajectory |>
  pivot_longer(c(lma, hmat), names_to = "trait") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(trait), scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000)) +
  labs(x = "Evolutionary time", y = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](canonical_equation_files/figure-html/path-time-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Seen in trait space, the path is an L. Each point is one accepted step of
the stepper, and the steps grow long once only the slow direction is left:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(ce$trajectory, aes(lma, hmat)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = final, colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Leaf mass per area, lma", y = "Height at maturation, hmat")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](canonical_equation_files/figure-html/path-space-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The red point is the evolutionarily stable strategy. It is the same
attractor that `community_solve_singularity()` finds directly, as described
in [Finding evolutionary attractors](solving_attractors.qmd). The canonical
equation adds the route there, and the test for branching on arrival.
